episodes.195373: A couple of thunderstorms produced gale-force wind gusts near Tangier Sound.
episodes.195607: Heavy rain due to tropical moisture and enhanced lift around the Blue Ridge Mountains caused excess water to runoff into the south Fork of the Shenandoah River. This led to flooding around Waynesboro. Additional flooding took place on the east side of the Blue Ridge Mountains across Albemarle County as well as northern Nelson County.
episodes.195887: Tropical Storm Helene caps off a several day heavy rainfall event in association with a stalled closed upper low that drew a stream of tropical moisture into the area on the 25th and 26th. The arrival of Helene on the 27th yielded catastrophic flash flooding and river flooding, as well as significant wind damage as wet soils and strong wind gusts led to forest damage.
episodes.196429: Thunderstorms moving offshore produced strong wind gusts along the Brevard County Coast.
episodes.196694: Tropical Cyclone Helene began organizing over the western Caribbean on the 23rd and 24th of September before rapidly intensifying as it moved north through the eastern Gulf of Mexico on the 25th and 26th. A plume of moisture extending from the intensifying storm interacted with a slow-moving cold front to produce a band of widespread heavy rain showers and embedded scattered thunderstorms over the southern Appalachians and vicinity on the 25th and 26th, resulting in a predecessor heavy rainfall and flash flooding event over these areas. Helene made landfall in the Florida Big Bend and moved quickly N/NE through Georgia before turning toward the N/NW once the remnant center reached northeast Georgia. Tropical rainbands around the center of Helene swept over areas with already-saturated soils over the mountains and foothills during the early morning of the 27th, resulting in extreme rainfall and record, catastrophic flash flooding across multiple basins with headwaters near the Blue Ridge escarpment. Due to its quick movement, Helene was still a strong tropical storm when the wind field reached the western Carolinas and northeast Georgia. Frequent wind gusts of 55 to 70 mph, with occasional gusts of 80 mph...and likely as high as 100 mph across the higher elevations combined with saturated soils to produce widespread damage to trees and electrical infrastructure. Across the mountains, some east and southeast-facing slopes above 3000 feet saw canopy-loss of 80% or more. Hundreds of trees fell on houses, vehicles, and power lines throughout the area, resulting in several fatalities. Almost all customers in several counties lost power for at least a brief period. Most people were without power for at least a couple of days, while thousands were without power for a week or more.
episodes.201070: At the surface, a low moved north-northeastward from northwestern IN to southwestern Lower MI during the early afternoon through late evening of the 24th. This allowed the trailing cold front to sweep eastward across IN toward the IN/OH border, while the warm front drifted northeastward across northern OH, much of southern Lower MI, western and central Lake Erie, and portions of northwest PA. Within the warm and moist sector, scattered multicell thunderstorms persisted northeastward and eastward over western and central portions of Lake Erie during the early evening. These storms generated isolated gale-force straight-line wind gusts in the Port Clinton, OH area amidst moderate effective bulk shear and MUCAPE, respectively.

events.narrative: Although heavy rainfall ended across Burke County during the afternoon, flooding continued along upper portions of the Catawba basin through much of the 28th. While most of the tributaries returned to their banks by early morning of the 28th, major flooding continued along the Catawba itself through the morning as water from widespread very heavy rainfall filtered its away downstream through the watershed. Numerous roads and structures remained inundated during this time, and this portion of the river didn't fall below flood stage until the afternoon.

events.narrative: A wind gust of 34 knots (39 MPH) was measured by the Lower Hooper Island WeatherFlow sensor (XHPR).

The massive flood wave on the Nolichucky River entered the eastern half of Greene County. Nolichucky Dam crested at 66.03 feet during the early morning of the 28th, setting a new record crest by far. Justified concerns that Nolichucky Dam would not withstand the flood wave were fortunately eased as the dam withstood the onslaught, although the power station building was damaged beyond repair. Downstream, the river gauge at Lowland just outside of Greene County shattered its previous record crest by 9 feet, cresting at 35.16 feet at 10:15 am EST on the 28th. Numerous structures were flooded or destroyed. Numerous roadways were inundated and some bridges were destroyed.

The water level along the South River at Harrison above the flood stage of 9.5 feet, cresting at 12.11 feet around 2:45 AM EST on the 28th. Trixie Lane was flooded and water approached homes near the river.

Flooding on the Cocke County side from the massive flood wave on the Nolichucky River near Lowland. The Lowland river gauge was above its previous record crest for nearly 20 hours, cresting at 35.16 feet at 10:15 am EST on the 28th, 9 feet above its previous record. Damaging flooding occurred, but in mostly rural and agricultural areas. As the river swelled out of its banks in the area where it becomes the border between Greene and Cocke counties, it flooded Goodwater Road around midnight where an elderly couple were swept away in their vehicle trying to escape. All told, Cocke County estimates $24.3 million in total county damages, which are included in the entry for the Pigeon River record flooding.

Flooding on the Hamblen County side from the massive flood wave on the Nolichucky River near Lowland. The Lowland river gauge was above its previous record crest for nearly 20 hours, cresting at 35.16 feet at 10:15 am EST on the 28th, 9 feet above its previous record. Damaging flooding occurred, but in mostly rural and agricultural areas.

The water level along the South Fork of the Shenandoah River, cresting at 17.65 feet at 1:30 PM EST on the 28th. Farmland on both banks of the river began to flood between Lynwood and Port Republic. Water covered Flank Circle in Lynnwood and approached homes in the area. Portions of the Power Dam Road and Captain Yancey Road between Lynnwood and Berrytown were also flooded.

Although the water was in the process of receding during the morning of the 28th, significant flooding continued along the Catawba River from Lake James to the Catawba County line through much of the day, and didnt completely fall below flood stage until the morning of the 29th.

TVA increased releases from Douglas Dam for a few days in response to incoming flood waters from the Nolichucky, French Broad, and Pigeon Rivers. Flooding due to backwater issues caused by the high releases included Tuckahoe Creek, impacting Smith School Road and Kodak Road. Flooding also reported along Curtis Road. Some sections of roadways were flooded a foot deep.
A section of Bingham Road near the 9200 Block along the South River was closed due to flooding.

Several Roads remained flooded in the eastern portion of August County. Over a half a foot of water was reported over Jericho Road in Staunton and a foot of water was over the Bridge on Shalom Road near J and B Lane.
